title: A Whole Life Given Over
overview: Paul turns from explaining God's mercy to describing the kind of life that grows out of it, in how people think, treat each other, and respond to enemies.

parts.label: A living sacrifice (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Looking back on the mercy he has described in earlier chapters, Paul borrows the picture of temple sacrifice: instead of a slaughtered animal, people offer their whole living selves to God. He asks them not to simply copy the ways of the world around them, but to let their thinking be made new from the inside.

parts.label: One body, many gifts (vv. 3-8)
parts.note: Paul warns against an inflated view of yourself and pictures the community as one body whose parts have different jobs but belong to each other. The abilities he lists, from inspired speaking (prophecy) to teaching, giving, leading and showing mercy, are all described as gifts freely given, to be used well rather than boasted about.

parts.label: Love that is real (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: Love should be genuine, not a performance, and people should try to outdo one another in showing respect. Hospitality here means taking in traveling strangers, a real need in a world with few inns and believers who sometimes faced hostility.

parts.label: Blessing and shared feelings (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Wishing good on people who hound you echoes Jesus' teaching to love enemies. Paul also asks people to share in each other's joys and griefs, and to spend time with those of low standing instead of chasing status.

parts.label: No revenge (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: Paul forbids paying back harm with harm, quoting the Hebrew scriptures to say that settling scores belongs to God, not to the injured person. The image of heaping "burning coals" on an enemy's head comes from Proverbs, and its exact meaning is uncertain.

disagreement: Christians read the "burning coals" of verse 20 differently: many see kindness that brings an enemy to shame and change of heart, while others see it as kindness that leaves an unrepentant enemy more accountable before God's judgment.
think: When someone has wronged you, what do you think actually breaks a cycle of harm instead of keeping it going?
